summary: Specifies an SDP grouping mechanism for RTP media streams that signals the association between SDP media descriptions and WebRTC MediaStream and MediaStreamTrack concepts.

plainLanguage.summary: Name tags that match each audio or video piece to the right call stream.

questions: how does sdp identify webrtc media streams
what does the msid attribute look like
subtitle: The msid SDP attribute that tells a WebRTC peer which MediaStream and track each media description belongs to.

tldr.problem: In WebRTC, media arrives as RTP streams described in separate SDP media descriptions, but nothing in SDP or RTP says which MediaStream each track belongs to.
tldr.mechanism: A new media-level SDP attribute, msid, carries a MediaStream identifier plus an optional MediaStreamTrack identifier. Offer/answer procedures say how endpoints create, update and end streams and tracks from it.
tldr.outcome: Endpoints can signal the grouping of tracks into streams over SDP. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and is not obsoleted or updated.

today: RFC 8830 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2021. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and IANA has registered the msid attribute.

sections.title: Why a New Mechanism Is Needed
sections.content:
Each RTP stream is identified inside an RTP session by its SSRC, and sessions are told apart by transport. SDP can describe many media descriptions, and under the WebRTC model each describes exactly one media source. Several sources share an RTP session only if BUNDLE is used. The SDP Grouping Framework (RFC 5888) can group media descriptions, but WebRTC also needs application-level information about the link between a media description and its group, which that framework cannot give.

The WebRTC API communicates using MediaStreams, which contain MediaStreamTracks. A track is unidirectional, carries audio or video but not both, and is generally carried on a single SSRC. Neither the RTP CNAME nor the RTP session corresponds to a MediaStream, so the association must be signaled explicitly.
sections.plainLanguage: The network only knows about separate pieces of audio and video. Nobody says which pieces go together in one call stream, so we need a label that says so.

sections.title: The msid Attribute
sections.content:
RFC 8830 defines a media-level SDP attribute named msid. Its value is an identifier and an optional appdata field, separated by a space:

msid-value = msid-id [ SP msid-appdata ]
msid-id = 1*64token-char
msid-appdata = 1*64token-char

Both are ASCII token strings of 1 to 64 characters. The identifier uniquely identifies a group within the scope of an SDP description. A media description may carry several msid attributes, which means one track is in several MediaStreams; the appdata MUST then be identical in all of them. Several media descriptions with the same id and appdata are not permitted. An example value is msid:examplefoo examplebar.

The attribute depends on how streams map to media descriptions, not to transports, so its Mux Category (RFC 8859) is NORMAL. An msid that does not match the grammar SHOULD be ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: The tag has two parts: the name of the box (the stream) and, optionally, the name of the crayon (the track). Each can be up to 64 simple characters.

sections.title: How Streams and Tracks Map to msid
sections.content:
The msid-id is the id of a MediaStream, and the special value of a single hyphen means no MediaStream. The msid-appdata, if present, is the id of a MediaStreamTrack. Across SDP updates, an id keeps referring to the same stream or track. There is no memory beyond the current descriptions: an id that disappears and later returns refers to a new MediaStream.

High-level rules for the recipient of an updated description:

  • A new identifier other than the hyphen can be signaled to the application as a new MediaStream.
  • New appdata values under an identifier can be signaled as new tracks added to that stream.
  • An id without appdata means the sender did not name the track, and the recipient assigns the track id itself. All such ids in one media section refer to the same track.
  • When a media description no longer lists any msid, the track can be signaled as ended.

A track also ends when all its SSRCs disappear (an RTCP BYE or a timeout under RFC 3550) or when the media description is disabled by setting its port to zero. Changing direction with sendonly, recvonly or inactive does not end it.
sections.plainLanguage: If a name tag shows up that nobody has seen, you open a new box. If a crayon's tag vanishes from the list, that crayon is gone.

sections.title: Offer/Answer Procedures
sections.content:
Detailed procedures follow RFC 3264 and describe actions on streams and tracks, leaving application events to JSEP (RFC 8829).

  • Offer: for each media description with an outgoing track, add one a=msid per MediaStream the track belongs to. The identifier is the stream's id, and the appdata is the track's id if the sender wants to signal it.
  • Processing: for each a=msid, find or create the track (by appdata), find or create the MediaStream (by identifier), add the track to the stream and tell the user a new track is available.
  • Answer: generated exactly like the offer, and offer values do not influence it. The offerer processes the answer exactly like an offer.
  • Modification: later exchanges repeat the same steps, plus a check: any existing track whose id no longer appears as appdata in an a=msid is stopped, setting it to "ended".

For packets that arrive with no signaled stream, the recipient creates a track from the media type, uses the MID header extension if present to find the media section, and waits until the connection is in RTCSignalingState "stable". It then uses the msid if there is one. Otherwise the track gets a random id and joins a stream with the WebIDL label "Non-WebRTC stream". Implementations that limit the buffering this needs MUST tell the user that media was discarded.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides write tags the same way and read them the same way. If a tag is missing, the receiver waits until things settle and then makes up a name.

sections.title: Example SDP
sections.content:
The RFC's example shows a PeerConnection with two MediaStreams, each holding one audio and one video track. Only the msid parts are shown. The two media descriptions of the first stream share the same identifier (starting 47017fee) but have different appdata (the track ids), and the second stream uses a different identifier (starting 61317484).

The pairing of identifier and appdata is what makes each media description unique, matching the rule that no two media descriptions may repeat the same id and appdata.
sections.plainLanguage: Two boxes, each with one audio crayon and one video crayon. Boxes share a box name, and every crayon has its own name.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
An attacker who can modify SDP can switch tracks between MediaStreams. This is a special case of the general rule that SDP changes must be confined to entities the application trusts. Buffering of unsignaled media should be limited to avoid memory exhaustion attacks.

Careless generation of identifiers can leak privacy-sensitive information. The W3C media capture specification recommends building identifiers from a UUID of class 3 or 4, which avoids this. The RFC identifies no other attacks that depend on the mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone who can edit the name tags could put crayons in the wrong box, so tags must only be edited by people you trust. Do not put your personal info in the names.

sections.title: Rejected Alternatives
sections.content:
Appendix A lists ideas that were not adopted. Using the RTP CNAME was dropped because CNAME identifies a synchronization context, and tracks from one context might need to be in several MediaStreams, while tracks from several contexts cannot be in one MediaStream since a stream imposes synchronization on its members.

Putting the msid in an attribute of RTCP sender reports was rejected because it does not let you know you have seen all the tracks configured for a MediaStream. A generic MSID with semantics set by an a=wms-semantic attribute survived several drafts but was removed in April 2015.
sections.plainLanguage: Other ways of labeling were tried, but each one either mixed up the groups or could not tell when all the crayons were counted.
